label: grafana-dashboards-observability-en
top_ai_sentences: Each piece of the dashboard has a specific job.

**Rows** group
related panels into collapsible sections and keep the layout tidy.

Pick the one that matches
where your team already handles alert routing.

**Variables** let people filter by
service, route, or interval without touching the query text.

Use $__rate_interval
rather than a fixed window so the query tracks the zoom.

This recipe walks through wiring a data source, building a
dashboard with panels and variables, provisioning it from disk, and adding alerts.

**Terraform** manages the dashboard as real
infrastructure, just like the rest of your stack.

The Prometheus UI is good for ad-hoc queries, but it doesn't build
full dashboards.

This is useful when your team wants one screen for request rate, latency, and
error rate across the fleet, with on-call engineers spotting failing services
quickly and non-technica

Recording rules pay for themselves when
the same expensive PromQL shows up on several dashboards.

Grafana connects natively to Elasticsearch, InfluxDB, CloudWatch, Loki,
Jaeger, and plenty of others.

It also works when you want dashboards stored as code and rolled out
through Git.

Avoid grouping by high-cardinality labels in
overview panels.

**Alerts** run PromQL
expressions and send notifications through Grafana or Alertmanager.

Querying months of data on an overview
dashboard is wasteful, so set a sensible default range.

Fifty panels on one dashboard is too many, and the page gets sluggish and
unreadable.

If you leave dashboards
editable in the UI after they're provisioned, any change disappears on the next
restart.

A Grafana dashboard turns a heap of Prometheus metrics into a live, readable view
of your services.

**Provisioning** pulls dashboards from disk whenever Grafana starts, so they live
in Git and rollbacks stay simple.

Grafana is purpose-built for visualization, with dozens of panel types, variables,
and layouts.

A variable that lists every pod in a large
cluster can drag query performance down.

Keep them fast with recording rules, a sensible default range, limited variables,
and a low maxLines cap for Loki.

Match the refresh interval to the use case:
five seconds when you're live-debugging, thirty seconds to one minute for
overviews.

Cap Loki maxLines
at a few hundred to avoid dumping huge result sets into the browser.

**Panels** turn PromQL queries
into tables, graphs, gauges, or stat tiles.
